messages.subject: Re: AKDE for a herd
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris (& Robert),

The method you mention for adding a spatially constraining term sounds interesting. I have a similar problem--I'm running RSFs for birds that are central-place foragers, so they are constrained by distance to the nest (although they can still fly shockingly far). Right now I'm running an RSF model that includes a "distance to nest" parameter. Is this what you mean by adding spatially constraining term to the model?

I'm not sure how this concept can be used in the generation of "available" environment. As I understand, the available environment is usually based on some a priori defined extent, often the animal's home range. I think this is what Robert was describing in his question. Then, you generate a bunch of random points (or, if using a point process, a grid of points), within the area that you've defined as the available extent to define the available environment. How is it possible to avoid this step using the method you described?

Is there perhaps a paper with an example of how to do this? I think that would be really helpful!

Thank you,

Ben

On Friday, February 22, 2019 at 6:19:32 PM UTC-5, Christen Fleming wrote:
> Hi Robert,
>
> I would avoid that route and instead try to add spatially constraining terms to the model, as is done in "synoptic" home-range estimation. This effectively adds a smooth notion of availability (really, it is site fidelity now) that is fit to the data simultaneously with the covariate dependence, instead of a (typically) discontinuous spatial constraint that is chosen a priori. Also, fitting the spatial dependence first, as is typically done with MCP->RSF, doesn't allow the model to completely tease apart the two influences, and so robs the covariates of some of their explanatory power.
>
> Just make sure your data satisfies the IID assumptions when doing RSFs. If you need to thin the data but want to use all of the data, then you can run all possible coarsenings of the data and average the results together (without shrinking the standard errors).
>
> Best,
> Chris
>
> On Friday, February 22, 2019 at 4:03:48 PM UTC-5, Robert Ritson wrote:
> >
> > Hi Chris,
> >
> > I am starting an RSF analysis for my bison herds and would like to define the extent of area used by multiple individuals within a single herd. I would like to use AKDE instead of the traditional MCP. Will the 'overlap' tool help me to define the area used by all the individuals (which I already calculated AKDE for) or should I recalculate AKDE using all the GPS points together? I was wondering what you would recommend. Thanks in advance for your help!
> >
> > Sincerely,
> >
> > Robert Ritson

messages.subject: Re: AKDE for a herd
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

"distance to nest" is one possibility, though you might want to try different powers. E.g., square distance to nest gives you a Gaussian in the absence of covariates.
Hi Ben,

There are different ways to integrate the RSFs/SSFs. One way is to sample uniformly over the "available" region, but this necessarily presumes a finite "available" region, which is a model choice.
A better way is to sample with a pilot density, if you have one. Say your RSF depends on square distance to nest, like this

RSF(x) = exp(-(x-nest)^2/(2 Sigma))/(2 pi Sigma) exp(-beta*covariates(x)) / Normalization

where nest, Sigma, beta are the parameters of your model and

Normalization = integral exp(-(x-nest)^2/(2 Sigma))/(2 pi Sigma) exp(-beta*covariates(x)) dx

but note that this is the same as the expectation value

< exp(-beta*covariates(x)) >_p

with respect to the pilot density

p(x) = exp(-(x-nest)^2/(2 Sigma))/(2 pi Sigma)

The "available" region can now formally extend to infinity without divergence, but when drawing random locations from p(x) you tend to sample a concentrated region around the nest.

As for references to people that do this, I would try the "synoptic home range" literature, but I don't really recall their numerics. I know I've seen this kind of trick used with in SSFs, but there its mostly for fitting the step & resource parameters simultaneously. The first paper I know of that did something like that was Avgar's integrated SSF paper.

There really should be a canonical reference on different methods to perform the RSF/SSF integration. Most RSF/SSF papers don't even explain that the random sampling is a Monte-Carlo approximation to the normalization integral.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: AKDE for a species around human development
messages.subject_clean: AKDE for a species around human development
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I study wood turtles and I have been using the akde to calculate their home ranges.

My problem is that my study site is partially surrounded by housing development and when some of my home ranges are calculated it shows that the turtle could be using those areas.

I understand that it could be possible for a turtle to wander into these areas(so I cannot input a barrier), but it is not very likely since there is barely any ideal habitat on the other side of the development.

I have included some photos of the turtle relocations and the akde home range populated from the points.Turtle 20 is fairly accurate but turtle 12 and 19 expand into the housing development.

Any thoughts on how I can incorporate the development into my code to possibly get a more accurate home range?

Thanks, Shaylyn

messages.body_plain:
Hi Erin,

The mean location is already estimated in the fit object: FIT$mu

The mode location you can find from the UD object either at the maximum of UD$PDF or (equivalently) at the minimum of UD$CDF. These are both 2D arrays. The grid locations are stored in UD$r$x and UD$r$y.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Why is occurrence function taking long time and have not yet to produce results?
messages.subject_clean: Why is occurrence function taking long time and have not yet to produce results?
messages.body_plain:
I am only using first 500 data points consisting of animal GPS coordinates and DOP values which is put in an telemetry object.  Also keep in mind that the data was irregularly sampled (contisting of several cycles of 5min, 30min, and 4hr intervals). I created a model which was fitted via variogram.fit() then ctmm.fit().  However when I run the model using occurence function, it seem to taking too long, taking around 30 hours until I decided to stop it.

Any tips on how to shorten that processing time?  Here's the code that I was using:

# Convert time to POSIXct objects
LHdata[,timestamp := as.POSIXct(LMTdatetime.GPS.rounded, tz=timezone)]

# telemetry assumes Movebank naming conventions.
# Sufficient MoveBank columns include:
#
#   individual.local.identifier
#   timestamp
#   location.long
#   location.lat
#
# If DOP values are to be included, the column name should be "GPS.DOP"
LHdata[,individual.local.identifier := UNIQUE_ID]
LHdata[,location.long := Longitude]
LHdata[,location.lat := Latitude]
LHdata[,GPS.DOP := DOP]
LHtele <- as.telemetry(
  object = LHdata,
  timezone = timezone
)

# Create and fit a variogram model (which should be stored in GUESS)
SVF2 <- variogram(LHtele,dt=dt)
variogram.fit(SVF2)

# Fit a ctmm model.
FIT2 <- ctmm.select(data = LHtele, CTMM = GUESS)

# Compute occurrence distribution
UD <- occurrence(LHtele,FIT2)  # This one seem to be taking forever

messages.subject_clean: Kriging occurrence to fill in missing locations
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

As a newbie to ctmm and overall movement modeling, I apologize in advance for my ignorance with this topic.  I read your paper "where and how animals move" with great interest, especially with how the kriging occurrence appears to resolve the missing points to a greater integrity than other methods.

My collars were set to sample in alternating bouts of 5 minute fixes and 30 minute fixes over a 12 hour period daily.  Within the good dataset, there are some few missed sampling fixes.  Can the ctmm kriging occurrence be used to interpolate and fill in those missing points, or does the ctmm occurrence only work on regularized sampling intervals?

However, within my bad data due to missed sampling fixes and lost collars, a large chunk of my data has irregular sampling periods ranging from fixes every 14 minutes to fixes every 18 hours.  Can I use the ctmm occurrence to fill in the missing times in these gaps to give it a regularized trajectory that I can use to work with?

Thanks in advance!

Hi Vincent,

I suspect its the gaps. Occurrence distributions of all types are very sensitive to large gaps in the data. Large gaps take longer to fill in (computationally) and even then they just produce a big blob because you don't know where the animal was during the gap. So the output would not look good even if you waited for the calculation to finish. There are two arguments in occurrence() to skip gaps: dt.max and cor.min:

https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/occurrence.html

I was going to type some recommendations for reasonable arguments, but I just went ahead and updated the development version of the package on GitHub to have more better/tighter default arguments. You can upgrade via:

devtools::install_github("ctmm-initiative/ctmm")

Please see if that helps.

Best,
Chris

On Sunday, March 31, 2019 at 12:28:26 AM UTC-4, Vincent Stowbunenko wrote:
> I am only using first 500 data points consisting of animal GPS coordinates and DOP values which is put in an telemetry object.  Also keep in mind that the data was irregularly sampled (contisting of several cycles of 5min, 30min, and 4hr intervals). I created a model which was fitted via variogram.fit() then ctmm.fit().  However when I run the model using occurence function, it seem to taking too long, taking around 30 hours until I decided to stop it.
>
> Any tips on how to shorten that processing time?  Here's the code that I was using:
>
> # Convert time to POSIXct objects
> LHdata[,timestamp := as.POSIXct(LMTdatetime.GPS.rounded, tz=timezone)]
>
>
> # telemetry assumes Movebank naming conventions.
> # Sufficient MoveBank columns include:
> #
> #   individual.local.identifier
> #   timestamp
> #   location.long
> #   location.lat
> #
> # If DOP values are to be included, the column name should be "GPS.DOP"
> LHdata[,individual.local.identifier := UNIQUE_ID]
> LHdata[,location.long := Longitude]
> LHdata[,location.lat := Latitude]
> LHdata[,GPS.DOP := DOP]
> LHtele <- as.telemetry(
>   object = LHdata,
>   timezone = timezone
> )
>
>
> # Create and fit a variogram model (which should be stored in GUESS)
> SVF2 <- variogram(LHtele,dt=dt)
> variogram.fit(SVF2)
>
>
> # Fit a ctmm model.
> FIT2 <- ctmm.select(data = LHtele, CTMM = GUESS)
>
>
> # Compute occurrence distribution
> UD <- occurrence(LHtele,FIT2)  # This one seem to be taking forever
>
>
